scenario: A luxury-wealth survey samples only households with net worth above $2 million because lower-net-worth households opt out of the premium advisory panel. An economist wants the mean net worth across all households in the source population.

data.description: Only households above $2 million are observed. Net worth is modeled as Normal with known standard deviation sigma = $1.5 million.

question: Using the truncated normal model, estimate (a) the true mean net worth mu across all households in the source population and (b) the fraction of households that appear in the premium advisory panel.
naive_answer: The typical household in the source population has net worth around $2.71 million because that is the panel mean.
naive_trap: The panel is an extreme upper-tail sample. It excludes more than 90% of households, so the panel mean is not even close to the population mean.
reasoning_trace: Step 1: Solve 2,705,502.5 = mu + 1,500,000*lambda((2,000,000-mu)/1,500,000). Step 2: The solution has alpha about 1.3, so mu = 2,000,000 - 1.3*1,500,000 = 50,000. Step 3: The panel fraction is sf(1.3) about 0.0968.
python_verification:
from scipy.optimize import brentq
from scipy.stats import norm
def eq(mu):
    a=(2000000-mu)/1500000
    return mu + 1500000*norm.pdf(a)/norm.sf(a) - 2705502.5
mu=brentq(eq,-5000000,1999999)
frac=norm.sf((2000000-mu)/1500000)
assert abs(mu-50000)<40000 and abs(frac-0.0968)<0.005
